_readme.title: The Remnant Continent — Ashland Conquest encounter content, consolidated (rev 2)
_readme.contents: 18 settlement/world encounters, 11 field encounters, 35 quests, 131 beats, 89 prereqs, 383 choices, 1133 effects. Supersedes remnant_content_consolidated.json — that file's content is carried forward unchanged except where noted under applied_in_this_pass.

applied_in_this_pass.new_content: 9 new quest chains and 4 new world encounters added. Goldgrass: q_notes, q_seasons, q_hire. Free Plainers: q_baron, q_claim, q_haulers. Two-beat placed encounters: q_glass, q_wire, q_road. Settlement encounters: we_standard, we_castmark, we_reading, we_beam (flavor-only).
applied_in_this_pass.relic_payout: ef_cro_rel_gg_gain retuned 8 -> 6 per direction. This is the only existing row modified by this pass.
applied_in_this_pass.dropped_before_authoring: A drafted 'q_lot' (disputed common well between two holdings) was cut — it duplicated we_assize, which is the same dispute over the same object.

known_breaks_pre_existing.sold_bunker_to_versari: Read inside we_petition's triggerStrength conditional and written by nothing. The encounter still fires; it silently takes the fallback weight forever. Present in the source file, NOT introduced here. Needs a writer or the branch removing.
known_breaks_pre_existing.ch_cro_blowback_ack: Sets a flag and adjusts standing but neither advances nor completes q_croppers, so the quest never closes on that path. Present in the source file. q_baron now consumes its blamed_for_barons_war flag, but does not fix the missing COMPLETE_QUEST.
known_breaks_pre_existing.ch_cro_relic_plainers: Effect ordinals are [0,2] — a gap where a row was removed. Cosmetic, present in the source file.
known_breaks_pre_existing.ch_cro_relic_goldgrass_standing: Grants goldgrass +4 for handing over the relic, while ch_cro_relic_return grants +6 for withholding it against an explicit Goldgrass claim. Reads inverted. Unresolved — flagged, not changed.

required_systems.recurring_yield: HIGHEST PRIORITY. qb_not_4_settled, qb_sea_4_bound, qb_hau_3 and ch_std_fund all want a per-round yield; three earlier encounters already did. Seven total. Authored as fixed QUEUE_DEFERRED chains, marked with _note, to be collapsed when the effect lands.
required_systems.count_flags: Now load-bearing, not optional. ch_clm3_install gates on count_flags{prefix:'rule_'} >= 2; ch_clm4i_hard / ch_clm4i_soft split on count_flags{prefix:'rule_hard_'} >= 2. Until it exists, ch_clm3_install never offers and qb_clm_4_installed is unreachable. q_road and we_standard and we_reading were written partly to pad the rule_* tally so the big ruling chains are not carrying it alone.
required_systems.honor_menace: ADJUST_HONOR and ADJUST_MENACE are still listed engine-only in the authoring guide. Usage has grown from 19 effects to well over 70. Promote to builder-editable or the majority of this content's moral consequences import untunable.

world_encounters.title: The Assize
world_encounters.text: Two households have come before your seat, and both are right. The well between their holdings was dug by one family three generations back and has been kept clear by the other ever since. The old claim is documented. The labor is undeniable. They have stopped speaking to each other and started speaking to you.
world_encounters.art: A stone well between two fenced plots; two families standing apart, a seated figure between them.

world_encounters.title: Winter Ledger
world_encounters.text: The stores were counted twice because the first count was not believed. There is no thief and no enemy in this. The yield was short, the season is long, and the arithmetic does not resolve itself no matter how it is arranged on the page.
world_encounters.art: A grain floor swept nearly bare; tally marks chalked on a post.

world_encounters.title: The Fever House
world_encounters.text: It started in the low quarter and it has not stopped there. Four dead in nine days, and the number of houses with a closed door is growing faster than the number of dead. People are still going to work. People are still coming home.
world_encounters.art: A narrow street of shuttered houses, one door marked in chalk.

world_encounters.title: What the Diggers Found
world_encounters.text: A foundation crew broke through into a sealed room beneath the settlement. Not a cellar. The walls are lined with dead panels and the cabling runs out of the room in every direction — into the streets, into the works, into everything you depend on. Something down there is still drawing current, and the crew will not go back in.
world_encounters.art: A concrete chamber lit by a single lamp; banks of dark panels, cable trunks disappearing into the walls.

world_encounters.title: The Levy
world_encounters.text: You need bodies under arms and the settlement has a finite number of them. Every name on the list is a name that is currently doing something else.
world_encounters.art: A muster table in a square; a queue of people who do not want to be in it.

world_encounters.title: The Petition
world_encounters.text: They came in daylight, through the front, with a written list. Not a mob — a delegation, chosen by the quarters, polite to the point of insult. They do not want grain or coin. They want a say in who you deal with beyond these walls, and what you promise, and what you give away.
world_encounters.art: A delegation of townspeople in a hall, one holding a folded paper; no weapons anywhere.

world_encounters.title: The Man From Downriver
world_encounters.text: He came upriver with a full boat and prices that do not make sense. His papers are almost in order — the kind of almost that is a decision rather than an accident. He is not nervous. He has done this before, and he does not intend to explain the gap between what these goods cost and what they are worth.
world_encounters.art: A flat-bottomed boat at a plank landing, crates under oiled canvas, a trader with his hands behind his back.

world_encounters.title: The Naming
world_encounters.text: A child born in the low quarter is named for a place instead of a person — a town three days east that has not existed for a century, which this family came out of four generations back. The grandmother insisted and would not be moved. The parents are embarrassed about it and did it anyway.
world_encounters.art: A naming gathering in a small room; an old woman holding an infant, younger parents standing behind.

world_encounters.title: The Argument About the Wire
world_encounters.text: Two of your people are shouting at each other in the works over a salvaged coil. One wants it unwound for the copper, which is worth something today. The other insists it is part of a thing, and should be kept whole until somebody works out what the thing was. Neither can name it. They have had this argument before, in these words, and neither of them actually wants it settled.
world_encounters.art: A workshop bench with a large salvaged coil on it; two people arguing across it.

world_encounters.title: The Thanksgiving
world_encounters.text: The eastern quarter holds its harvest rite at the field edge — grain laid out in a pattern, a little water poured, a fair amount of singing. It is over inside the hour. You are invited as a courtesy and it is plain that nobody minds either way whether you come.
world_encounters.art: A small gathering at a field edge at dusk, grain laid on cloth, a poured vessel.

world_encounters.title: The Woman Who Wouldn't Sit
world_encounters.text: A visitor to your hall declines the offered chair and stands through the entire meeting, close to the wall, and leaves without remarking on it. Afterward your steward mentions that some Readers won't settle in a room they've only just entered. Or that it isn't that at all and she simply doesn't care for chairs. He is honest that nobody actually knows which.
world_encounters.art: A hall meeting; one figure standing near the wall while everyone else is seated.

world_encounters.title: The Reader at the Gate
world_encounters.text: She came in on the morning road and asked at the gate for your seat by name. She offers to sit with you before your next decision — not a prophecy, she is careful about that, just the shape of what she feels coming, and she will tell you plainly when she is unsure. Your settlement knew she was here before you did and is watching what you do about it.
world_encounters.art: A woman waiting in a settlement gate-yard with a travelling bag; people watching from doorways.

world_encounters.title: The One You Caught
world_encounters.text: Your people took an armed man well inside your holdings — not in a fight, just found where he had no business being, with a story that fell apart the second anyone checked it. He may be a scout. He may be a thief. He may be a man who got badly lost and is too proud to say so. He has given a name, and the name is not the one he gave yesterday.
world_encounters.art: A man seated on a stool in a storeroom, hands loose in his lap, two guards at the door.

world_encounters.title: The Steward's Post
world_encounters.text: The man who ran your stores died in the night, at his desk, of nothing in particular. The post is open and the settlement has opinions. Your own kin wants it and would be loyal and unremarkable. There is a woman in the third quarter nobody has heard of who is said to have a head for it. And there is always the option of paying for someone from outside who has actually done this before.
world_encounters.art: A store-room office; ledgers stacked on a desk, an empty chair pushed back.

world_encounters.title: The Standard
world_encounters.text: The builder wants to make one window frame a hundred times rather than a hundred frames once. It costs more up front, it means turning away three joiners who each have their own way of doing it and each of whom does it well, and it means every window in this settlement will be identical for as long as the settlement stands. He is not romantic about it. He has the arithmetic and it is correct. The three joiners are also in the room and they have arithmetic of their own.
world_encounters.art: A workshop floor with one jig and a stack of identical frames; three older joiners standing apart with their own work.

world_encounters.title: The Cast Mark
world_encounters.text: A Laker casting comes in with the trade goods — a swollen curved bracket with raised numerals formed in the mold, no seam ground off the back, doing in one piece a job that three of your bolted-together parts have been doing badly for years. Your smith has spent two days with it and can tell you precisely how it was made and precisely why he cannot do it. He would like to be sent east to learn. He is forty-one and he is your only smith.
world_encounters.art: A heavy cast bracket on a workbench beside three flat bolted parts; a smith turning it over.

world_encounters.title: The Reading
world_encounters.text: There is a woman in your settlement who reads people and places, openly, for a stated fee, as a trade like any other trade. This week two households took a dispute to her instead of to your seat. She heard it, told them what she saw, and they accepted it and went home, and consider the matter closed. Nobody has broken any law. There is simply now a second place in this settlement where things are decided, and it has a shorter queue than yours.
world_encounters.art: A front room with two chairs and a table; two households leaving, satisfied.

world_encounters.title: The Names on the Beam
world_encounters.text: The new granary's ridge beam goes up carved with the number of every crew that worked it — no names, just the counts, cut deep, because that is how it is done and has been done since anyone here can remember. Somebody has added one more number at the end. It does not correspond to any crew on the roll. Nobody will say what it stands for and nobody appears to think it is a problem, and the beam goes up with it.
world_encounters.art: A ridge beam being raised, deep-cut numerals along its length; one extra numeral at the end.

field_encounters.title: The Man Who Won't Give a Name
field_encounters.text: He has been camped at the edge of your holdings for a week. Armed, alone, and careful about it — the fire is small, the horse is picketed where it can be reached, and nothing has gone missing. He has not approached anyone and he has not moved on. When your people ride out to him he stands, waits, and gives them nothing at all.
field_encounters.art: A low fire at the treeline at dusk; a standing figure with a covered blade, a picketed horse behind.

field_encounters.title: The Silo
field_encounters.text: You see it for half a day before you reach it — a grain elevator standing alone with nothing around it for miles. Empty inside, and swept. Someone repaints the ladder rungs. The inner wall is carved over with names going back four generations, packed close and overlapping, and one of your plains riders takes out a knife and adds his own without asking anyone or explaining why.
field_encounters.art: A lone concrete grain elevator on flat ground; carved names covering an interior wall in the light from the door.

field_encounters.title: The Ledger at the Bridge
field_encounters.text: The only bridge for a day in either direction, and sitting at the near end of it is a Versari factor with a table, a ledger, and no guards whatsoever. He is entirely unworried. The crossing has a price, and he would rather write an obligation into his book than take anything off you today. He explains the terms clearly and fairly and does not press.
field_encounters.art: A trestle bridge over a cut river; a folding table at the near end, a man with an open ledger, no escort.

field_encounters.title: The Reader at the Crossroads
field_encounters.text: She sits under an awning at the settlement's only junction with a painted board and a small stated fee, the way a farrier or a scribe would. She reads the road ahead for travelers. The queue is four people long and nobody in it finds this remarkable.
field_encounters.art: A woman under a canvas awning at a crossroads, a painted board beside her, travellers waiting.

field_encounters.title: The Hulk
field_encounters.text: A landship on blocks outside a frontier town, being lived in. A stovepipe punched through the deck plating, laundry strung from the rigging points, two families and a great many children. The drive has been dead for thirty years and there is nobody within four hundred miles who could bring it back.
field_encounters.art: A beached landship hull on timber blocks, stovepipe smoke, laundry lines, children on the deck.

field_encounters.title: Wrong Water
field_encounters.text: A Laker trader camped on the near bank of a ford, unloading nothing, going nowhere. The water is low and clear and looks entirely ordinary to every one of your people. He says it isn't right today. Pressed, he says it again, in the same words, and goes back to his fire.
field_encounters.art: A shallow ford in flat light; a trader's camp on the bank, wagon unhitched, nobody crossing.

field_encounters.title: The Tattooed Man
field_encounters.text: A Versari scholar travelling alone with his sleeves rolled against the heat, both forearms marked wrist to elbow in bands and figures. Asked, he explains readily — this band a discipline, this one a rank held for eleven years, this one a debt since discharged and marked as such. He seems mildly disappointed that out here a man's whole career can be written on his arms and nobody can read a word of it.
field_encounters.art: A traveller's forearm in close view, banded institutional tattoos from wrist to elbow.

field_encounters.title: Goldgrass Notes
field_encounters.text: The trader at the waystation prices everything in Goldgrass notes — printed, numbered, signed at a hall three hundred miles east by someone whose name he says as though you should know it. He takes them from strangers without hesitation. He has never been to the hall and does not expect to go.
field_encounters.art: Printed paper notes weighted under a stone on a trestle table beside sacked grain.

field_encounters.title: The Ashfall Year
field_encounters.text: The old woman at the waystation starts talking before anyone asks her anything. The year the sky went orange, she says — not the old catastrophe, a smaller thing, sixty years back — and the wheat came up wrong for three seasons after. She is precise about the dates and vague about everything else. Her grandchildren have heard it a hundred times and find work to do in the other room.
field_encounters.art: An old woman at a hearth in a waystation kitchen, talking; younger figures leaving through a doorway.

field_encounters.title: The Foundry Boy
field_encounters.text: A Laker apprentice, fifteen at the outside, minding a wagon of pig iron alone on an open road. He has been sent overland from Chigan and is visibly proud of it. Given the smallest encouragement he will explain his works' entire pour schedule, the names of everyone on his shift, and what he intends to be doing in ten years. Nobody has told him the plains are dangerous.
field_encounters.art: A young man on a loaded iron wagon on an empty road, entirely at ease.

field_encounters.title: The Ones Who Don't Answer
field_encounters.text: A frontier holding close enough to the trail that you pass within fifty yards. Smoke from the chimney, stock in the pen, and someone standing at a window watching your column go by. Your people call out twice. Nobody comes out. Nobody waves. There is no sign at all that anything is wrong.
field_encounters.art: A sod-and-timber holding beside a trail; a figure at a window, unmoving.

quests.title: The Debt of a Dead Man
The Wrong Side of the Weather
The Assembly Learns to Say No

quest_beats.text: A work gang is laying rail across a gap in the old line — perhaps a mile of missing track between two intact stretches, which is the difference between a dead corridor and a live one. There are no faction markings on anything. They have tools, a little iron, and not enough of either. The foreman doesn't ask. She just keeps working while she talks to you.
quest_beats.art: A gap in old rail with fresh ties laid; a mixed crew working without banners.

quest_beats.text: The gang has moved down the line and the gap behind them is closed. The foreman recognizes your colors before she recognizes your face. They can finish from here, she says, and she means it as thanks rather than dismissal. Come back when it's done. There'll be something worth seeing.
quest_beats.art: Closed track running to the horizon; a crew packing tools onto a handcart.

quest_beats.text: The last spike went in two days ago. The foreman explains what this was always for: a line no faction owns, open to any trader who keeps the peace on it, because a corridor that everyone can use is a corridor nobody has to fight over. She has been looking for someone to help hold it that way.
quest_beats.art: A finished junction with a plain unpainted marker post; no flag on it.

quest_beats.text: The bison are moving north and it is the wrong season for it. They are not grazing as they go. Half a mile on, your scouts find carcasses — a dozen, scattered rather than dropped in a line, none of them opened the way a predator opens an animal. Nothing has fed here. They simply stopped.
quest_beats.art: Prairie under high cloud; a bison herd pressed northward, dark shapes on the grass behind them.

quest_beats.text: A family on the same heading, moving faster than their cart should allow, with the doors of their old life still open behind them. They will take water. They will not take rest. Pressed, the woman says a witch put something on their settlement and everyone who stayed is still there. She believes every word. She cannot tell you one thing she saw with her own eyes.
quest_beats.art: An overloaded cart on an open track, a family walking beside it, looking north.

quest_beats.text: The route south is open and empty. Whatever the herd came out of is that way, three days at your pace, and nobody is going to make you look at it. Your own people have opinions and are keeping them to themselves.
quest_beats.art: A fork in a prairie track; the southern branch running into flat grey haze.

quest_beats.text: He flags you down on the open road, recognizes your colors, and produces a tally-stick split down the middle — his half notched against a half held by a man of your faction who has been dead two years. The arrangement was real. The obligation was never discharged. He has been carrying this stick a long way.
quest_beats.art: A road-side trader holding a split hazel tally-stick, notches visible along its edge.

quest_beats.text: He is still on your route, a day behind and making no secret of it. Other traders on this road have heard the story by now, and the story has already decided which version of you it prefers. Nobody has said anything to your face.
quest_beats.art: A camp of trade wagons at dusk; conversation stopping as a column passes.

quest_beats.text: The matter has resolved itself, one way or the other, and the road has an opinion about it now.
quest_beats.art: A settlement gate with traders gathered; a tally-stick on a table.

quest_beats.text: The front comes in fast and low and there is nothing between you and it. The one piece of ground worth having — a cut bank with an overhang and a windbreak already built — is occupied. Half a dozen scouts, another faction's colors, equally caught, equally aware of what the next six hours look like out in the open.
quest_beats.art: A cut bank under a black wall of storm; two small parties looking at each other across open ground.

quest_beats.text: The storm takes most of the night. There is nothing to do in it but wait, and waiting with people is not the same as waiting near them. Somebody's name gets learned. Somebody says more than they meant to about where they've been ordered and why.
quest_beats.art: Firelight under an overhang; two groups sharing the light, not quite mixed.

quest_beats.text: You meet one of them again, well away from that ground and in better weather. He recognizes you before you place him, and whatever he does next was decided months ago on a night neither of you has mentioned since.
quest_beats.art: A rider halted on a road, hand visible and empty, recognizing someone.

quest_beats.text: A surveyor working alone, unhurried, with instruments that are older and better than anything your people carry. He is not lost and not in trouble. He will trade copies of his work for passage and for not being robbed, and he says both parts of that sentence in the same tone.
quest_beats.art: A lone figure at a plane table on a rise, instrument case open, horses grazing.

quest_beats.text: What he produced is better than you expected — grades, fords, the two crossings your own scouts had wrong. It is also, you learn, not exclusively yours. He sells to everyone. And somewhere in his case is a sheet with your holdings on it, drawn with the same care.
quest_beats.art: An unrolled map on a table, weighted at the corners, fine hatching for terrain.

quest_beats.text: He comes to you first, which he did not have to do. He intends to sell the sheet of your territory and he is asking whether you object. He has already priced your objection.
quest_beats.art: A folded map sheet held out across a table; two people not touching it.

quest_beats.text: A landship wreck, long dead, stripped of everything obvious years ago. But the frame is sound — good structural iron in lengths nobody can cut new — and hauling it out is a season of slow work rather than an afternoon of luck.
quest_beats.art: The ribbed hull frame of a landship half-sunk in grass, plating long gone.

quest_beats.text: The crew that arrives has been working this wreck for a season. Families, not soldiers — cutting gear, a windlass, a camp with children in it. They consider the wreck theirs by use rather than by right, and they know exactly how a fight would go. They say so plainly, which takes more nerve than a threat would.
quest_beats.art: A scavenger camp beside the wreck; cutting rigs, laundry lines, a windlass.

quest_beats.text: You cross paths with them again, and what they are to you now was settled at the wreck.
quest_beats.art: A work crew on a road, tools on their shoulders, recognizing a column.

quest_beats.text: Your comms officer brings you a set you don't recognize the traffic on. It's keyed from inside the settlement you're passing, on a band nobody in your outfit uses, and whoever is sending knows the equipment better than the people who own it. A man's voice. He gives a location, a name, and the fact that he is not free to leave. He does not ask twice and he does not beg. He explains his situation the way a man explains a fault in a machine, and then he goes quiet, because staying on the air any longer would cost him.
quest_beats.art: A field comms set on a wagon tailgate at dusk; an operator with one hand on the dial, the settlement wall in the distance.

quest_beats.text: He is what your grandfather's stories called a wire-reader, and there are perhaps a few dozen of them alive between the lakes and the mountains. He can make old-world equipment answer. That is why he is held and that is why the people holding him have talked themselves into believing they aren't holding him. How you go about this decides everything that follows, and you will not get to try twice.
quest_beats.art: A hand-drawn plan of a settlement's wall and gate, weighted with a knife.

quest_beats.text: You send in a request under your own colors, plainly worded, naming him. Admitting they hold him is worse for them than negotiating over him — so they will not refuse outright. What they do instead depends entirely on what your word is worth on this side of the continent.
quest_beats.art: Two delegations at a gate table, a written request between them, nobody sitting.

quest_beats.text: You go in for him. From this point it is a military problem with a man somewhere inside it, and the failure you should be afraid of is not losing the fight.
quest_beats.art: A column moving on a settlement gate before first light.

quest_beats.text: Contact first, then timing, then a night. Your people are inside for three days before anything happens at all, which is how this is supposed to work. He is a good partner in it — he understands sequence, and he does exactly what he is told exactly when he is told to do it.
quest_beats.art: A lamp in a shuttered window; a figure counting on a gate watch's rotation.

quest_beats.text: He is out, and sitting across from you, and the immediate danger is behind both of you. He is a smaller man than the voice suggested, with burn scars on both forearms and the flat calm of someone who has already survived the worst version of this. He asks what you want from him. It is a real question and he is prepared for any answer.
quest_beats.art: A man in a borrowed coat at a camp table, hands flat on the boards, waiting.

quest_beats.text: The work is good. Nobody could say otherwise. He is at the bench when they open it and at the bench when they close it, and what he builds runs. He has stopped asking about the guard on the door. He has also stopped maintaining the small brass set he arrived with, which sits on the shelf getting dusty, and the man who noticed didn't think to mention it.
quest_beats.art: A workbench under a lamp, tools squared away; a small brass comms set on a shelf, untouched, dust on the dial.

quest_beats.text: They found him in the morning at the bench, and everything he was working on was finished and labelled and left in order, because that was the last thing he could decide about. Word of it will travel. There are very few of these people and they know each other's names.
quest_beats.art: A finished workbench, tools laid straight, every part labelled; an empty stool.

quest_beats.text: It didn't work. He is alive, moved somewhere deeper in that settlement, and under a different kind of watch now. He also knows somebody came. On this continent that is not nothing.
quest_beats.art: A shuttered upper window with a new bar across it.

quest_beats.text: He did not survive it. Whatever else this cost you, that is the part that will be remembered by the only people who could have replaced him.
quest_beats.art: A collapsed roof section, smoke going flat in the wind.

quest_beats.text: A Versari supply train on the eastward run to Dambar — six wagons, a thin escort, and a route that says they were not expecting to be seen out here. Your patrol is upwind and unobserved. Whatever happens on this stretch of road, there is nobody to say afterward that it was you.
quest_beats.art: A short line of covered wagons on a rutted road, escort riders strung out, dust hanging behind them.

quest_beats.text: One of the men who was on that road comes to you privately, and he is not nervous, which tells you he has thought about this. He would like more than his pay. He is not asking for much and he is very clear that he is only asking once.
quest_beats.art: A soldier standing at ease inside a command tent, cap in hand, entirely calm.

quest_beats.text: The train reaches Dambar intact and your unit is thanked properly, in front of people, which costs the Dambarans something to do. Over the meal it comes out sideways: the crops failed last year and are failing again this year, and nobody can say why. They are glad of Versari aid. They are noticeably less glad to be in Versari debt, and the man who says so does not look at anyone while he says it.
quest_beats.art: A high stone hall in thin mountain light; a table of Dambaran officials, a Versari seal on a crate behind them.

quest_beats.text: Word comes down from the high city. What you sent held them through the worst of it and did not hold them through the rest. They ask for as much again, and the asking is plainly costing them more than the grain is worth.
quest_beats.art: A written request under a Dambaran seal, delivered by a tired rider.

quest_beats.text: Your man inside the Versari capital reaches you on a band he should not still be using. He believes his cover is gone. He also believes he is a week from the truth of it, and he is asking you to make that week possible. He does not say which of those two facts he wants you to weigh more heavily.
quest_beats.art: A cramped room above a street, a hand-built set on a table, one lamp turned low.

quest_beats.text: You tell Dambar that the inquiry is over. They take it without argument and with obvious grief, and they thank you for having tried, which is worse than if they had been angry.
quest_beats.art: An empty council table; one man still seated after the others have gone.

quest_beats.text: He has it. Whether you ever hold it in your hands depends entirely on whether he can get himself out of a city that has been watching him for a fortnight.
quest_beats.art: A city gate at night seen from a rooftop; two watchmen and a long open street.

quest_beats.text: Your patrol rides into the end of something. Bodies across forty yards of ground, several days old, and everything worth carrying already carried. What is strange is the absence: no blades left in the dirt, no fittings on the carts, not a nail. Somebody stripped the metal specifically. One of your riders has seen this before and gives it a name — Steel Traders — and points out the tracks going west.
quest_beats.art: A scatter of carts on open ground, wheels stripped to bare wood, tracks leading away.

quest_beats.text: Goldgrass farmers, all of them, and the loads on the carts say they were bringing a harvest to market rather than carrying anything worth killing over. Your people count the dead twice. There is no head man among them, and a party this size does not travel without one.
quest_beats.art: Grain spilled and rotting in a cart bed; a tally being kept in a notebook.

quest_beats.text: The tracks end at a wall built out of the old world — haulers and freight vehicles dragged into a ring, cut down, welded and packed with earth until the whole thing became a fort. A man on the rampart watches your unit come the last half mile and lets you get close enough to hear him before he asks what you want.
quest_beats.art: A rampart made of stacked and welded old-world hauler bodies; a lone figure standing on it.

quest_beats.text: You bring what you know to the nearest Goldgrass hall — the dead, the missing head man, and the ring of welded haulers a half day west of here. They listen the whole way through without interrupting, which is not how these people usually receive news.
quest_beats.art: A Goldgrass hall, a map weighted flat on a trestle table, a dozen people standing over it.

quest_beats.text: You go back with the Goldgrass at your shoulder and considerably more of them than you expected. This time nobody on the rampart asks what you want.
quest_beats.art: A combined column at dawn approaching the hauler-wall; smoke already rising from one section.

quest_beats.text: An envoy of Clan Tempest is at your gate with a small escort and no gifts, which is itself a message. He does not state his business to your steward. He says only that his clan believes you are the sort of power that can be of use to them, and that he would rather say the rest to your face.
quest_beats.art: A Laker envoy in storm-grey at a settlement gate, three riders behind him, no banner.

quest_beats.text: By Grand Laker tradition the right to rule sits with Clan Tempest, and by the arithmetic of five rival clans it sits with a coalition that has closed the capital to them. He does not argue the tradition; he assumes you know it. What he wants is your weight on the scale. What he offers is a share of what falls out of the city, and Tempest at your back on the day you need it.
quest_beats.art: A Laker envoy laying out a chart of the lake ports on a table.

quest_beats.text: The call comes from the siege lines outside the Laker capital. Tempest has committed everything it has and it is not going to be enough on its own. They are asking, plainly, for how much of your strength you will put in front of that wall.
quest_beats.art: Siege works outside a lake-port city; earthworks, ships standing off the harbour.

quest_beats.text: The siege ends the way sieges end, and the accounting begins immediately.
quest_beats.art: A breached gate; two banners on the same wall.

quest_beats.text: The Lakers receive what you send them and act on it inside a day. They pay you for it, correctly and without warmth, and the man who hands over the scrap makes a point of not shaking your hand. They know exactly what they bought and from whom.
quest_beats.art: A Laker quartermaster counting out scrap on a dockside table.

quest_beats.text: Forty or fifty Croppers in a hollow in the middle of open country, well away from any road, standing in a formation that is plainly not a camp. There is singing. Their wagons are drawn up at the edge of the hollow and there is nobody near them. You cannot make out what they are actually doing from here.
quest_beats.art: A ring of plains folk standing in a shallow hollow at dusk, wagons drawn up behind them.

quest_beats.text: You are seen a long way out and they have you ringed before you have finished explaining yourself. They are furious in a way that is entirely about the interruption and not at all about you — this was a rite to the goddess of the fields, it has a season and an hour, and you have spent both. Since you have taken something from them, they say, you will give something back.
quest_beats.art: A unit ringed by unarmed farmers on open ground, close enough to touch.

quest_beats.text: From the ridge you can see the whole of it, and there is nothing in it to be afraid of: grain laid in a pattern, water poured out, a great deal of singing. It is a harvest rite and it is entirely benign. You can also see, from up here, that every last one of them is facing the hollow and not one of them is facing the wagons.
quest_beats.art: A view down into the hollow from a grass ridge; unguarded wagons in the foreground.

quest_beats.text: Baron Juan holds a walled estate with more men on it than the title suggests, and he does not deny having the relic. He is amused that farmers sent soldiers. He is willing to discuss it, and he is equally willing not to.
quest_beats.art: A fortified plains estate, wall guns visible; a well-dressed man on the steps.

quest_beats.text: It is a plough iron, very old, worked with figures along the beam and worn smooth in the places a thousand hands have held it. It is also, you learn from a Goldgrass factor who takes far too much interest in it, a thing the Goldgrass have wanted back for two generations and consider theirs by an older claim than the Croppers'.
quest_beats.art: An ancient worked plough iron on a blanket, figures visible along the beam.

quest_beats.text: Whatever Baron Juan did with your people, he did it against another Plainer leader, and he did it under colors that were not his own. The main body of the Free Plainers is not confused about whose troops those were. Nothing you say about the arrangement improves the situation.
quest_beats.art: A Plainer war council; a captured banner on the table that is not the Baron's.

quest_beats.text: The assembly uses its seat for the first time and blocks a passage agreement you had already shaken hands on. The objection is procedural, correct, and entirely within the authority you gave them. The man who delivers it has clearly been practising.
quest_beats.art: A hall table with a written objection on it; a delegation standing, a seat empty.

quest_beats.text: This time it is not a passage agreement. They block something you need, for reasons that are defensible and not, in your judgment, correct. You gave them this. Taking it back is a thing you can physically do in an afternoon.
quest_beats.art: A crowded hall, a vote being counted on a slate.

quest_beats.text: The outside world has worked out what happened, because it always does. Envoys arriving this season are behaving differently, and the difference is precisely calibrated to what you did in that hall.
quest_beats.art: A foreign envoy at a settlement gate, addressing a delegation rather than a seat.

quest_beats.text: A man from that quarter is back after four years away, with a trade, a decent reputation from two settlements downriver, and a request for work. He is polite about it. He was behind the line, or in the camp, depending on what you did, and he does not raise it and does not need to.
quest_beats.art: A man in travelling clothes at a hiring table, papers in hand.

quest_beats.text: He is good at the work. He is better than the man above him, and everyone in that quarter has quietly worked out who to actually ask when they need something done. Nothing improper has happened. Your appointee is simply being routed around.
quest_beats.art: A queue of people outside a small workshop office, ignoring the larger office next to it.

quest_beats.text: He asks for the post outright, which is the first thing he has asked for. Granting it makes formal a situation you created the day you closed that street. Refusing it is also an answer, and the quarter will read it correctly within a week.
quest_beats.art: A man standing across a desk, hat in hands, entirely composed.

quest_beats.text: Word arrives from the people who fed you through the bad season. It is not a demand and it is careful not to look like one. It is a courtesy: they will be asking, before long, and they wanted you to hear it from them first.
quest_beats.art: A sealed letter on a table beside an unopened grain tally from a previous season.

quest_beats.text: The ask arrives and it is genuinely inconvenient. Passage through your territory for something you would rather not have crossing it, on a timetable that is theirs and not yours. They are entirely within their rights to ask and they know exactly what they are asking.
quest_beats.art: A map with a corridor drawn across held territory in another hand's ink.

quest_beats.text: The debt is closed either way. What it closed into is the thing that will matter for the rest of this war.
quest_beats.art: Two seals on a single closed page.

quest_beats.text: He asks for something, which he has never done. Materials, a quantity of your time, and a room he does not have to share. He will say it is a project and will not say what the project is, and he is plainly aware of how that sounds and asks anyway.
quest_beats.art: A tidy workbench with an empty cleared space at its centre; a written list of materials.

quest_beats.text: Someone in your administration reports, carefully, that what is being built in that room is not what was described. It is not a weapon and it is not dangerous. It is simply his, and it was never yours, and the person reporting it is not sure why that bothers them.
quest_beats.art: A part-built apparatus under a cloth, wire runs going up the wall to a roofline.

quest_beats.text: Asked directly, he tells you immediately and without defensiveness. It is a set built to reach the others — the handful of people alive who can do what he does, scattered through every faction and largely unknown to each other. He has been assembling the list for eleven years. He was always going to tell you. He was waiting to be asked.
quest_beats.art: A completed transmitter and a hand-written list of names, most of them crossed through.

quest_beats.text: The stores are short and have been short for a while. It is small, consistent, and it predates whoever holds the post now — the pattern runs back into the dead man's own hand. Somebody has been doing this for years and nobody caught it because nobody was looking.
quest_beats.art: Two ledgers open side by side, a finger on a column that doesn't reconcile.

quest_beats.text: The trail resolves, and where it goes depends on who is holding the books now and what this seat has taught people it rewards.
quest_beats.art: A store-room at night, a lamp, a hand lifting a floorboard.

quest_beats.text: There is no hall for this and no crowd. Just you, a room, and a person who knows what you know. Whatever you decide here, only a handful of people will ever be certain what happened, which is a different kind of decision than the one you make at the assize.
quest_beats.art: A small closed office; two chairs, one lamp, the ledgers stacked between them.

quest_beats.text: The thing she described begins happening, and it is close enough to her wording that the people who were in the room that day notice, and the people who weren't hear about it by the end of the week.
quest_beats.art: A settlement street; two people talking, one gesturing back toward the hall.

quest_beats.text: Your settlement has started going to her first. Not instead of you — before you. She did not seek this and is visibly uncomfortable with the size of it, and it happened entirely because your seat sat down with her in the open where everyone could see.
quest_beats.art: A queue outside a small door; the hall behind it comparatively quiet.

quest_beats.text: She tells you, in the hall, in front of everyone, that what you intend is going to go badly. She is not performing and she does not enjoy it. Every person in that room is now watching to find out whether this seat takes counsel or only takes convenient counsel.
quest_beats.art: A full hall; a standing woman speaking, the seat opposite her, no one else moving.

quest_beats.text: A cut stone at a trail junction, recent work, marked with a figure nobody in your unit recognises. Once you have seen one you start seeing them — another at the next fork, another on a ridge line. They are placed by someone who expects them to be read, and they make a line if you are willing to spend the time following it.
quest_beats.art: A shaped marker stone at a trail fork, a carved figure cut sharp and recent.

quest_beats.text: The line ends at a place with nothing to recommend it — a dry creek bend under cottonwoods, no road, no water worth stopping for. There are eleven people there and they are waiting for somebody, and the somebody is not you. They are unarmed, unbothered, and quite clear that you have arrived early.
quest_beats.art: A gathering under cottonwoods at a dry creek bend; packs stacked, no wagons, no weapons.

quest_beats.text: An abandoned settlement, empty since long before anyone riding with you was born, and three new graves in the yard. Weeks old at the outside. Dug properly and deep, which took someone a long day's work. No names, no marks, nothing left behind. Whoever buried them did not stay.
quest_beats.art: Three fresh mounds of turned earth in the yard of a collapsed farmstead.

quest_beats.text: A family on the road going north, and one of them sees your colors at distance and reacts badly before getting hold of himself. They buried the people you found. Asked what of, they say they don't know, and it becomes clear over the next few minutes that this is the literal truth and it is the part that frightens them.
quest_beats.art: A family halted on a road with a handcart, one man turned half away.

quest_beats.text: A boy on a fast horse, twelve or thirteen, carrying sealed correspondence between two parties who are not you. He will tell you who it is from if you press him and he will not hand it over, and he is entirely clear about the difference between those two things.
quest_beats.art: A young rider halted on a road, satchel across his chest, hand on the flap.

quest_beats.text: The same boy, a year on and aged the way frontier children age. He is still running the same road and he is not running it for the same people.
quest_beats.art: The same rider, older, on the same road, a different seal on the satchel.

quest_beats.text: A man hauling salt alone, moving at night, on a route that touches no settlement between here and the river. Nothing is hidden in the load. Salt is simply worth enough now that this is how you move it. He would trade what he knows about the road for company through the dark stretch.
quest_beats.art: A single covered wagon on a night road, one lamp, one driver.

quest_beats.text: He finds you this time, which takes some doing, and he is carrying something he would rather not carry alone — a route, a settlement, a party moving where they have no business being. He gives it up for nothing. He is not being generous. He is putting it down.
quest_beats.art: The salt trader at a camp fire, talking, not eating.

quest_beats.text: A blind above the river crossing, built properly out of cut brush and sunk into the bank, with a clean sight line onto the ford and weeks of tally marks scratched into the back board. It is empty right now. Somebody has been counting everyone who crosses here since the spring.
quest_beats.art: A brush-built hide above a river crossing; tally marks cut into a plank inside.

quest_beats.text: This time the blind is occupied, and whoever is in it does not run — he has been sitting in a hole for four months and would rather explain than be dragged out explaining. He tells you who pays him without being pushed, because he has no particular loyalty to them and no reason to invent one. Then he waits to find out what you are going to do about it.
quest_beats.art: A young man sitting in the hide with a tally board across his knees, looking up.

quest_beats.text: The Versari scholar has been in your settlement four days and has spent most of them in the works, talking to one person — a young man who takes things apart and puts them back together improved, and who cannot explain to anyone how he knows what to do. The scholar wants to take him. Not to a school; there isn't one. He would travel with the scholar's party and learn on the road. There is no address to write to and no date he would come back. The scholar has already spoken to the family. He came to you afterward, and he made certain you understood the order of those two things.
quest_beats.art: A workshop interior; an older man in a travelling coat leaning on a bench watching a young man work.

quest_beats.text: The family comes to you and asks what you think, which is the worst thing they could have done. They will do whatever you tell them and they will hold you to it afterward either way. The boy is standing behind his mother and has clearly been told not to speak.
quest_beats.art: A family standing in a hall doorway; a young man behind them, saying nothing.

quest_beats.text: The party left before dawn and the works has not been the same since. Nobody has replaced him because nobody can. Years from now a trader will mention, in passing and without knowing why it matters, that there is a young Versari out on the western circuit who asks after this settlement by name. That is the entirety of what you will ever receive.
quest_beats.art: An empty stool at a workshop bench; tools laid out and untouched.

quest_beats.text: He is still at the bench and he does the work he is given. He has stopped bringing things to anyone unasked. Whatever he was going to be good at, he is being careful not to be good at it here, and everyone in the works has noticed and nobody has said it out loud.
quest_beats.art: A young man working steadily at a bench, not looking up, the room busy around him.

quest_beats.text: He comes back roughly when it was promised, which is more than you expected. He is markedly more capable and he is not entirely yours any more — he refers to the scholar's party as we without noticing he is doing it. He has also brought a second scholar with him, who spent the first afternoon walking your works and asking who made what.
quest_beats.art: Two travellers at a settlement gate; one young and familiar, one older and looking past him at the buildings.

quest_beats.text: The Versari factor arrives with a wagon, two guards, and a bound book he sets on the table before he sits down. He is not selling. He will advance what your settlement needs against a return at a later date, on terms he states plainly and does not offer to adjust. The terms are not unreasonable. He is entirely comfortable waiting while you work through them, and he does not fill the silence.
quest_beats.art: A trestle table in a settlement hall; a bound ledger, an inkhorn, a loaded wagon visible through the door.

quest_beats.text: It worked. Whatever you took did precisely what he said it would do, on the schedule he gave you. So he is back, with a larger wagon and a better offer — better terms than the first, not worse — because a settlement already written in the book is worth considerably more to him than one that is not. Taking it is obviously the correct decision. There is nothing hidden in it anywhere.
quest_beats.art: A larger wagon train at a settlement gate; the same factor, the same book, a fuller page.

quest_beats.text: Both entries come due in the same season, which is when you learn that the book compounds. What is owed is more than the sum of what you took. He turns the ledger around and walks you through the arithmetic line by line, and the arithmetic is correct, and he is not enjoying this any more than you are. He has a column ready for whichever answer you give.
quest_beats.art: The ledger turned around on the table, a finger resting under a total; two men on either side of it.

quest_beats.text: Your clerk gets a look at the open book while it is being packed, and what he sees is not an account of your settlement. It is an account of forty of them — who is solvent, who is short, who came through last winter on borrowed stores and will take any terms offered by spring. The Versari know the state of this continent settlement by settlement, in one hand, in one book, and not one of those settlements knows it about the others.
quest_beats.art: An open ledger showing page after page of settlement names, each with a running column.

quest_beats.text: There is a Laker crew on the scrap field and they have been there long enough to have poured a footing. Cutting rigs, a stack half up, a smelter under canvas, and something over forty people working. Nobody asked anyone. The foreman comes out to meet your unit wiping her hands, entirely friendly and entirely unapologetic, and points out that this iron has been lying here since before either of your grandmothers and nobody has cut so much as a length of it. She offers you a share of what comes off the line. She does not offer rent, because it has not occurred to her that rent applies.
quest_beats.art: A scrap field with a half-built brick stack and cutting rigs; canvas over a smelter, forty people working.

quest_beats.text: The first run comes off and it is plate, stock and fittings of a grade nothing in your holdings can produce and nothing you can buy within a season's travel. The foreman will trade it, and what she needs is specific: hands, food for forty and rising, and safe passage for the hauls going east. Every one of those is a real cost to you. The goods are worth it, which is the part that makes this difficult.
quest_beats.art: Stacked new plate and bar stock on a loading floor, still dark from the mill.

quest_beats.text: People out of your own settlements are working there now. Some of them have moved their families. There is a second stack, a cookhouse, a name painted on a board at the road end, and a woman who settles disputes without reference to anyone you appointed. It is a Laker town inside your territory and it arrived without a single soldier crossing your border.
quest_beats.art: A grown works town at dusk; two stacks, rows of housing, a painted board at the road end.

quest_beats.text: It is written down at last, on your terms, and your terms are worse than you would have set two years ago because two years ago there were forty of them and no stacks. The works answers to you on paper. The people in it answer to the woman with the board, and on most days those two facts do not collide.
quest_beats.art: A signed page on a mill office desk, weighted with a length of bar stock.

quest_beats.text: They go. It takes eleven days and they take the rigs, the smelter, the pattern boxes and every person who wanted to come, which is more of your own people than you had counted on. What is left is a scrap field with two dead stacks on it, and it will not be cut again in your lifetime. Somewhere on the lakes your name has gone onto a list kept by people who were already arguing that this is what the plains are like.
quest_beats.art: Two cold brick stacks over an empty cut yard; wheel ruts leading east.

quest_beats.text: It is on your map and it is not yours. It is profitable, it is peaceful, it trades with you on decent terms and with the lakes on better ones, and there is no document anywhere that says who it belongs to. Your riders go around it out of habit. Nobody has decided anything and everybody has adjusted.
quest_beats.art: A map with a settlement marked in a different hand than the rest of the sheet.

quest_beats.text: Your people stop working to watch it go past. Deep lacquer laid over original steel and rubbed back by hand until it holds the light, with patch plate let into the rear quarter where the body had rotted and the welds left standing proud because whoever did the work was not hiding it. It crosses broken ground your own units pick their way over. Four Lakers aboard, no cargo, nothing to sell. The driver slows enough to let your people look and does not stop, and one of your riders stands in the road afterward for longer than he needs to.
quest_beats.art: A restored pre-collapse vehicle on a plains road — dark lacquered body, welded steel patch panels, heavy off-road tyres, roll structure, racked cans.

quest_beats.text: It comes back through on a tow behind a flatbed, and the damage is to the body. Not the engine, not the axles — they can make those, and will. The rear quarter is torn open to the wheel arch and there is no such thing as a replacement panel anywhere on this continent, because the works that pressed it has been rubble for a hundred years. The driver will not look at it while they talk to you. He is taking it harder than he would take a wound.
quest_beats.art: The same vehicle on a flatbed tow, rear quarter torn open to the wheel arch, crew standing apart from it.

quest_beats.text: One of your own people mentions it that evening, almost in passing: there is a shell of the same make out in the rubble field, half buried, gutted decades ago for its mechanicals. No drivetrain, no glass, no interior. But the body is sound, and it has been sitting there worth nothing at all to anyone since before you were born. It is worth a great deal this week.
quest_beats.art: A half-buried body shell in a rubble field, sound but stripped, grass grown through the wheel wells.

quest_beats.text: The fabricator stayed the season, as agreed, and worked in the open where anyone could watch — and everyone did. Two vehicles came off the yard. Theirs, rebuilt around your shell. And a second, out of what was left over and what your people could make, and it is not as good and it runs. At the end of it he packs his tools, shakes hands all round, and goes east. You have something nobody else on the plains has, and no way at all to make another.
quest_beats.art: An open work yard; one finished lacquered runner and a second rougher build beside it, the crew standing back from both.

quest_beats.text: The factor sets up at the edge of your market on a Tuesday with a strongbox, a folding table and a clerk, and by Thursday there is a line. His name is Ilan Brey and he is from a hall three hundred miles east that you have never had occasion to think about. He is buying at prices nobody here has been offered in living memory and he pays on the day, in printed notes, numbered and signed. He is not asking your permission and he is not avoiding you either; when you come down to the table he stands up, greets you by your correct title, and offers you a chair.
quest_beats.art: A folding table at a market edge, a strongbox open, a line of farmers waiting; a clerk writing.

quest_beats.text: Your granary steward asks to keep his accounts in notes. He is not making an argument for anyone and he is faintly embarrassed to be raising it: converting back into barter is costing him something out of every transaction he handles, he has been eating that cost quietly for a season, and he would like to stop. He has the figures. They are worse than you expected.
quest_beats.art: A granary counting-room, ledgers open, a steward with two columns that do not reconcile.

quest_beats.text: Mother Sabine Orr comes in person, which Brey is careful to let you understand is unusual. The hall is prepared to extend credit against next year's harvest on terms that would take your worst season off the table entirely. She would be more comfortable, she says, if your grain land stayed in grain. She says it the way a person says something obvious and pleasant, and at no point does she suggest that there is an alternative, because from where she is sitting there is not one.
quest_beats.art: A hall factor in a quilted travelling coat seated across a table; a sealed credit book between two cups.

quest_beats.text: It is done quietly and nobody marks the day. Wages here are paid in notes, debts here are written in notes, and a farmer who has never been east of the river keeps his savings in a promise signed by a woman he will never meet. The arrangement is good. Your people are richer than they were. Brey has a house now, and an opinion about the drainage, and people ask him things.
quest_beats.art: A market square trading briskly, printed notes changing hands, a factor's house with a new roof.

quest_beats.text: There is no reprisal. There is no letter. On a Tuesday in the second month every note in your territory is presented for redemption at once — every hall, every factor, every waystation, on the same morning, by people who had no way of coordinating it and did it anyway. By evening your market is back to barter and your granary is worth what it weighs. Brey works the table all day and is perfectly civil to everyone, including you.
quest_beats.art: A market at dusk, a strongbox nearly empty, a queue of people holding paper.

quest_beats.text: The hall does not withdraw and does not punish; it simply stops growing here. Brey keeps his table and his prices and a good deal less of your economy than he had a season ago. What circulates in your market now is yours, backed by your stores, counted by your steward, and worth exactly what your word is worth — which is a harder currency to run and a currency nobody can call in.
quest_beats.art: A counting-house door with a plain unmarked tally box; a factor's table doing steady, diminished business.

quest_beats.text: The hall's factor comes out to the field edge with the schedule and reads you the relevant line without being asked to. His name is Emory Chelle and he holds a cutting contract on this harvest, taken out by whoever held this ground before you did, and it has passed to you along with the ground. The labor is Croppers, as it has been for forty years, priced in notes and honored on both sides without a written word ever passing between them. The cut falls on the fourteenth. So does the rite — it has a season and an hour, and this year the two land on the same day. He observes, pleasantly, that the weather after the fourteenth is the weather after the fourteenth. He does not tell you what to do. He does not need to: the hall is paid on the contract either way, and the grain in the field is yours.
quest_beats.art: Standing grain at a field edge; a factor with a schedule book; weather building on the west horizon.

quest_beats.text: The Croppers do not cut on the day. They are not defiant about it and they do not argue; they are simply not in the field, and not one of them can understand why this needs explaining. Their elder is a small woman named Nane Fisk who answers every question you put to her fully and courteously and does not once concede the premise. The grain is standing and the weather is turning.
quest_beats.art: An empty field at first light, tools stacked at the headland, nobody working.

quest_beats.text: The hall does not retaliate. It reprices. Cropper labor comes off the circuit — not banned, not denounced, simply quoted at a rate no hall between here and the river will meet — and forty years of custom ends as a line item in a schedule Chelle did not write and cannot amend. It is entirely rational and there is nobody to be angry at. Within a season they are landless, and they are landless on your ground.
quest_beats.art: Cropper wagons drawn up on open grass with nowhere to go; a hall schedule nailed to a post.

quest_beats.text: There is a Cropper population inside your territory now, permanently, working ground they do not own for a power they did not choose, and doing it well. They bring in more per acre than your own people ever did. They also bring a calendar, and the calendar has an hour in it, and every year for the rest of your life somebody will come to you in the second week of the month to confirm that the hour still stands.
quest_beats.art: Cropper families settled at a field edge; a marked post at the headland with no writing on it.

quest_beats.text: They are absorbed inside two seasons, which is the thing the Free Plainers are actually good at — not raiding, not holding ground, but taking in whoever has just been priced out of somewhere else and having them bolted on and load-bearing by spring. There are Cropper wagons in Plainer camps now with Plainer plate riveted to them. The rite is still performed. It is performed west of here.
quest_beats.art: A Plainer camp with newly joined wagons, mismatched plate riveted over old timber.

quest_beats.text: The rate holds. The Croppers cut for the halls again on the old terms and the custom survives with a piece of paper under it that never existed before, because you insisted there be one. Both sides now regard you as a party to their arrangement rather than as the ground it happens on, which is more standing than either of them meant to give you and more obligation than you meant to take.
quest_beats.art: Croppers cutting a field on a bright morning; a factor's schedule with an amendment pinned to it.

quest_beats.text: Plainer riders have hit four villages along this stretch since the thaw. Not burning them, which would be stupid — taking the season's surplus and enough draft animals to make next season harder, which is not. The hall has hired steel for the two largest towns and has run out of hall. The headwoman here is Anneke Dorn and she is perfectly clear-eyed about her position: ninety people, no wall worth the name, a fund the village raised out of its own pockets, and authority to spend it on exactly one thing. She would like it to be you.
quest_beats.art: A small farming village on open prairie, no wall; a headwoman at the road with a strongbox.

quest_beats.text: The riders work in a loose band of forty under a man called Sull, they are two days out and coming back on a pattern anyone could read, and Dorn has read it. What she cannot do is anything about it. How this goes is yours to decide, and she says so plainly and then stops talking, which is more discipline than most people manage.
quest_beats.art: A table with a scratched map of the district; a ford, a road, and four marked villages.

quest_beats.text: It is over inside a week, one way or another, and Anneke Dorn comes out to the road again to say whatever there is to say.
quest_beats.art: A village road at evening; a headwoman standing at the gate post.

quest_beats.text: Baron Juan sends a rider, unarmed and unhurried, with a message he has not bothered to have written down. He has heard that you wore the blame for a job he did under your colors. He is grateful. He is grateful in the specific way a man is grateful when the gratitude cost him nothing and the arrangement cost you a great deal, and he does not appear to see a difference between those two things. He has another one. Better paid. Same terms.
quest_beats.art: A lone unarmed rider on a road, waiting; a walled estate on the horizon behind him.

quest_beats.text: Colonel Reba Ives does not use the title and everybody else does. She lost eleven people and a season's stock to troops flying your colors and she has been told a story about you that she is willing to hear a different version of, once, in person, because she came up in a country where a man who rides in himself is worth listening to before he is worth shooting. She is direct about what she actually wants. It is not your soldiers. It is Juan, and it is your account of the arrangement, and of those two she can only get one from you.
quest_beats.art: A Plainer camp with a plate-patched command wagon; a woman at a plank table, listening.

quest_beats.text: It resolves the way these things resolve out here — not in a battle anyone names, but in who is still holding a gate at the end of the season. Whatever happens to Baron Juan, he knows which way you went. He has always been very good at knowing that.
quest_beats.art: A walled estate gate at dawn, seen from a distance; horses on the road below it.

quest_beats.text: The band on this ground runs to sixty families, a repair shop under a tin roof, and a standing pond somebody has bothered to fence. Tam Odell comes out to meet you, hears what you want, and negotiates it properly — he asks the right questions, he concedes the points he cannot hold, he does not haggle past the point of being taken seriously, and when it is done he shakes your hand and means it. He is entirely good for his word. He simply has no standing whatsoever to give it.
quest_beats.art: A Plainer camp around a fenced pond; a repair shop under tin; a man walking out to meet riders.

quest_beats.text: The Widow Ansel arrives with forty riders and a claim on this ground that predates Odell's by two generations. She was not consulted. She is not wrong, and she is not bluffing, and she does not accept for one moment that a price paid to Tam Odell has any bearing on anything. There is no court to take this to. There is no council. There is not even a custom, because a custom would require somebody to have been in charge long enough to establish one.
quest_beats.art: A second Plainer column arriving at a camp; two groups of riders facing each other, not yet fighting.

quest_beats.text: The third man is called Cutter. He has no title, no claim he has ever asserted, and forty people who have worked this ground continuously for eleven years while Odell and Ansel were establishing their respective rights to it. He has not come to be paid. He has come to find out what happens to his people under each of the men you have been handing money to, and he has evidently given the question more thought than either of them has.
quest_beats.art: A weathered man at the pond fence with working people behind him; two mounted parties waiting further off.

quest_beats.text: You hold the hex and everyone on it is content, and the arrangement rests on nothing except three separate men's satisfaction, none of which binds the others and none of which binds anyone who was not in the room. A fourth party will come. Not out of bad faith — simply because there is no instrument anywhere in this country by which the first three could have spoken for him.
quest_beats.art: A settled camp under new ownership; three separate groups keeping to three separate ends of it.

quest_beats.text: He is a leader now, in the sense that he has men and money and your backing and the other two have concluded that arguing is more expensive than not. Nobody has granted him anything. He is an authority in exactly the way a prop holds up a wall — completely, and only while it is there.
quest_beats.art: One Plainer leader on a plank platform with armed men behind him; two other groups watching from a distance.

quest_beats.text: The ground is yours and it stays yours, and that is the part worth sitting with. Three claims, eleven years of work, and sixty families amounted to nothing at all the moment somebody with a state behind him decided they did. Every people on this continent that eventually gets absorbed will get absorbed for this reason and no other, and none of them will see it coming, because from the inside the absence of a government looks exactly like freedom right up until the afternoon it doesn't.
quest_beats.art: An occupied camp; a fenced pond; new posts driven at the perimeter.

quest_beats.text: The ring of welded haulers is not a warband. It is a freight business. Forty vehicles, a yard, a fuel arrangement nobody will explain, and a man called Ledger who keeps the accounts and is the closest thing these people have to a government. He quotes you a rate to move bulk across the district that is below anything a Goldgrass hall will touch, and he quotes it in a way that makes clear he has already worked out what your alternatives cost. He is courteous, exact, and entirely uninterested in discussing anything except freight.
quest_beats.art: A yard of welded plate-bodied haulers; a man with a ledger at a plank desk under an awning.

quest_beats.text: Your quartermaster brings you a tarpaulin off one of the beds because he has recognized the repair on it. Once you are looking, it is not subtle: chain, tack, two grain hoppers and a pair of cart axles that came off the carts on that road, and the dates in Ledger's own book line up with the week those people died. He has not concealed any of it. It is stock. It was bought at a price and entered in the correct column.
quest_beats.art: A hauler bed with mismatched salvaged gear stacked on it; a farm cart axle among it.

quest_beats.text: Ledger sends word at the turn of the season, in the same hand he uses for invoices, confirming the standing of your account.
quest_beats.art: A plank desk under an awning; a ledger closed, an invoice weighted with a stone.

quest_beats.text: Forty acres of ground fused to green-black glass, flat as standing water, with grass growing right up to the edge of it and stopping. It is not a crater. There is no bowl, no rim, and no spoil anywhere — whatever did this did it downward without moving anything aside. A family has built a low house at the edge and grazes goats on the good side. They have been here eleven years and are entirely healthy. The mother mentions, without being asked, that nothing has ever grown on it, and that in high summer it is cold to the touch.
quest_beats.art: Forty acres of flat green-black glass meeting unbroken grass at a hard edge; a low house and goats at the margin.

quest_beats.text: Nobody can work it, cut it, name it or match it. It is not a material anybody on this continent has a use for, which does not make it any less obviously manufactured. A wire-reader passing through the district on somebody else's business walks out onto it, stands there for a long time, comes back, and declines to say anything at all — which is a great deal more information than any answer she could have given you. The family go on grazing goats.
quest_beats.art: A woman standing alone far out on a flat glass plain; goats and a fence in the foreground.

quest_beats.text: She travels with four armed people who are plainly not hers, and who are plainly not letting her out of their sight either. They were hired by the party that last employed her and they are retained until she is delivered to the next one. She is the scarcest thing on this continent and she is being moved like freight. She is bored, entirely professional, and openly willing to discuss her rates with you, since nobody has ever told her not to. She belongs to no faction and has no intention of acquiring one.
quest_beats.art: A woman on a road flanked by four armed riders in unmatched kit; her own horse plainly better than theirs.

quest_beats.text: Whatever you did, the party that hired the escort hears about it within the season, because hearing about it is what the escort was for. There is no authority to complain to and no penalty anybody can impose. There is only the fact that everyone who might ever need her now knows what happened on this road, and adjusts.
quest_beats.art: A waystation yard at dusk; riders exchanging a few words and moving on.

quest_beats.text: Two miles of pre-collapse roadbed running dead flat and dead true across broken country, a century on, with the drainage still working. Locals have been quarrying it for a generation. The cut stone is excellent and the holes are where you would expect them, and everything within four miles — walls, footings, a chapel, a byre — is built out of the road somebody is still trying to drive wagons along.
quest_beats.art: A flat engineered roadbed crossing rough ground, with sections pulled out for stone; a wall nearby built from the same material.

quest_beats.text: A season later the district has arranged itself around whatever you decided, in the unhurried way districts do. Nobody argued at the time. Everybody has an opinion now.
quest_beats.art: A stretch of old roadbed in whatever state it has been left in; carts on it or a wall built from it.

choices.label: Rule for the greater need
choices.outcomeText: The well goes to the household that cannot do without it. The other family says nothing in the hall and a great deal outside it. Word of the ruling travels faster than the ruling itself.

choices.label: Rule for the greater contribution
choices.outcomeText: The well goes to the household that kept it. The producers of this settlement take note of what your seat rewards, and work accordingly. Elsewhere, quieter people take a different note.

choices.label: Cut the ration
choices.outcomeText: The measure comes down and stays down. Nobody starves. Everybody notices, and everybody carries a little less than they did.

choices.label: Slaughter the draft stock
choices.outcomeText: The settlement eats through the cold. Come the thaw, everything that needs pulling will be pulled by people.

choices.label: Request aid
choices.outcomeText: The grain arrives. Nothing is asked for in return and nothing is written down, which is not the same as nothing being owed.

choices.label: Cordon the quarter
choices.outcomeText: The street is closed at both ends and stays closed. It works. The people behind the line know precisely who gave the order and how long it took them to give it.

choices.label: Open the stores to the healers
choices.outcomeText: They get everything they ask for, which is more than you expected them to ask for. The quarter comes through thinner and intact.

choices.label: Requisition a physician
choices.outcomeText: The physician arrives with a case of instruments, a written protocol, and no interest in the opinions of the household he is working in. His methods are resented and his results are not arguable.

choices.label: Move the sick outside the walls
choices.outcomeText: The camp is downwind and well out of sight, which was the point. It is called mercy by the people who built it and something else by the people carried into it.

choices.label: Study it properly
choices.outcomeText: Your researchers go down with a plan, a sequence, and instructions to touch nothing that is still live. It will take time.

choices.label: Open it with the crew you have
choices.outcomeText: The foundation crew goes back in with lamps and pry bars and a general theory. They are brave and they are guessing.

choices.label: Send word to the Versari
choices.outcomeText: The request goes east on the next rail. The reply is faster than you expected, which tells you something about how interested they are.

choices.label: Seal it and pour over it
choices.outcomeText: Rubble, then fill, then a slab. The crew is relieved. The room is still down there, still drawing current, and now nobody knows what it was.

choices.label: Take the young
choices.outcomeText: They march well and they will learn fast. The fields they came out of will be worked by people who are too old for it.

choices.label: Take the veterans
choices.outcomeText: You get a unit that knows what it is doing on the first day. You also take out every person who quietly holds a street together, and the settlement will not feel it until it needs them.

choices.label: Pay for frontier irregulars
choices.outcomeText: They arrive already armed, already competent, and entirely uninterested in your settlement. They will fight extremely well until a day arrives when fighting is not the best available option for them.

choices.label: Grant the seat
choices.outcomeText: They get a standing voice on anything you sign beyond the walls. Every foreign decision now costs a conversation. In exchange, this settlement will absorb a great deal of hardship before it cracks.

choices.label: Refuse them plainly
choices.outcomeText: You tell them no, in person, with a reason. They accept it the way people accept a thing they intend to raise again. Nothing happens today.

choices.label: Refuse them, and be heard
choices.outcomeText: You tell them no and they believe your reasons, because they have watched your seat rule for the people with the least to offer it. The list goes back in the pocket. They will wait.

choices.label: Deal with the leaders privately
choices.outcomeText: Three quiet conversations and three separate arrangements, and by the end of the week there is no delegation. There is also no version of this settlement that will ever bring you a list again.

choices.label: Try to deal with the leaders
choices.outcomeText: You make the offers. Two of the three refuse them in front of the third. They have seen your seat pick the profitable side before, and they came here expecting exactly this.
